4: This document provides evidence-based responses to the most common factually incorrect claims about Bitcoin mining and energy. It is an essential starting point for any regulator, policy-maker, journalist or curious individual who wants the facts about Bitcoin and energy. That means facts anchored in independent, up-to-date data about the Bitcoin network.
5: Every claim below was, at one time, common in mainstream media. As each was disproven, journalists stopped repeating it (not always immediately). Today these claims are largely no longer heard in mainstream media. The odd one still surfaces from time to time. For each claim I’ve noted where it came from, why it stopped, followed by what the evidence shows. I've also included a graphic at the top documenting when each claim went out of mainstream media circulation.
7: **Where it came from:** Alex de Vries’ five-page 2018 commentary in Joule. He divided Bitcoin’s total energy use by its number of transactions.
8: **Why it stopped:** Peer-reviewed studies rejected the method. Then in 2023, Sai and Vranken’s review found de Vries’ body of work unreliable. That left journalists with no credible source to quote.

16: For example, a whitepaper from Duke University energy experts looked at Controllable Load Resources (aka: Bitcoin mining). It concluded they help to [[10|stabilize grids]] and delay expensive grid upgrades.
20: These scholarly works are backed up by real world data from ERCOT. That is the grid which houses the largest concentration of Bitcoin mining.
21: One caveat: it is possible to use Bitcoin mining in a way that destabilizes the grid (just as it is possible to misuse a hammer to commit a crime). But when these instances happen, they are both mild and rare. For example, [[15|ERCOT (Texas) grid data]] shows Bitcoin mining stabilizes the grid almost daily. It does this through two different services: [[16|Frequency Regulation]] and [[17|Demand Response]]. There have also been several large-scale emergency events where Bitcoin mining stabilized the grid. The major documented case is Texas' [[18|July 2022 heatwave]]. In contrast, [[19|ERCOT has documented]] a small number of mild, local events. In these, mining loads briefly dropped off the grid during transmission faults. These nudged frequency up for a few minutes without causing any outages. So over a multi-year period, large-scale grid stabilization events far outnumber these brief disturbances.
24: **Why it stopped:** Brad Jones, ERCOT’s former interim CEO, [[21|said publicly]] that Bitcoin miners could meet ERCOT’s ancillary services, and that their ability to do so “at the lowest possible cost means lower costs for all consumers in the State of Texas.” The measured prices proved him right. After inflation, Texas household electricity prices stayed essentially flat once miners arrived.
27: Now let’s contrast this with Texas, the part of the US with an unusually high concentration of Bitcoin mining. In Texas, between 2021 and 2024, total electricity costs paid by residential customers rose from $21.23 billion to $26.29 billion (23.8%). That is 7.0% when adjusted for inflation.

47: Bitcoin mining is in fact the only global industry with robust, third-party data showing it has crossed the 50% [[37|sustainable energy]] threshold. The global average grid mix is about 41% low carbon, and other major sectors have no comparable industry-wide energy mix data. So it stands as a uniquely documented case of reaching this milestone at a global scale.
49: It is the generation of electricity that causes pollution, not the user of electricity. Like an EV, Bitcoin mining (sometimes called crypto mining) runs on electricity, so any pollution comes from how that electricity is generated. Over half of that electricity already comes from sustainable sources. Claiming Bitcoin mining causes pollution is as misleading as claiming EVs cause pollution. There is no universe in which it is logical to claim that Bitcoin mining causes pollution but EVs don’t. Nor is it logical to claim that EVs cause pollution but Bitcoin mining doesn’t. They are precisely analogous. If we find ourselves resisting this logical equivalence, that can help uncover our implicit biases.
50: EVs accounted for 80 [[39|Mt CO2e]] of attributable [[40|GHG]] emissions in China and the US alone. But this statistic is never presented in isolation. Similarly, it is highly misleading to present Bitcoin mining’s emissions without noting they are scope-2. It is equally misleading to leave out the more emission-intensive industry it replaces.
51: Cambridge data is very clear on this point. It attributes these emissions solely to scope-2 electricity use, not scope-1 direct impacts: “electricity usage of Bitcoin mining activity at approximately 138 [[41|TWh]], resulting in around [[42|39.8 MtCO2e attributable GHG emissions]]". That figure is similar to Bitcoin indirect emission levels in 2019.
56: **Where it came from:** Ethereum’s switch to proof of stake in September 2022. Greenpeace USA held it up as the model in its “Change the Code” campaign, demanding that Bitcoin do the same.
57: **Why it stopped:** Greenpeace USA’s campaign went silent in early 2024. It was [[47|reported as over in December 2024]], without a single line of Bitcoin’s code changing. By then, [[48|peer-reviewed research]] had shown that Bitcoin’s environmental benefits depend on proof of work. Proof-of-stake cryptocurrencies cannot deliver them.
66: The important point here is that conflating energy use with environmental harm is not only mistaken. It is something environmental scientists and a consensus of policymakers say we should avoid. Yes, when that energy use is mostly fossil fuel (as it is in the banking sector), more energy use is environmentally harmful. But when that energy use is mostly sustainable, more energy use promotes more climate action. That is the case when it helps mitigate methane and accelerate renewable energy development, as Bitcoin has been shown to.

82: **Why it stopped:** Energy researchers have since shown that short-run marginal emissions are not a credible way to measure the real impact of new electricity demand. In 2025, [[66|Bistline and Watten showed in Nature Climate Change]] that the method can overstate effects by 41–98%. Princeton’s Jesse Jenkins called it “NOT a credible measure of consequential emissions impacts.” Applied consistently, the same logic would say every electricity user takes renewable power from every other user. That would include a hospital, an EV owner or a heat pump.
84: But first, let's address the claim itself. The claim is unsupported by evidence. It also contradicts the built-in economic incentive of Bitcoin mining companies. That incentive discourages them from ever using power when wholesale power prices spike (when other people need it).
86: What there is strong evidence for is this. As a direct result of Bitcoin mining, many people now have access to renewable energy who otherwise would not.
87: For example, Gridless in Africa has delivered renewable energy to four villages (an estimated 28,000 people). On a much bigger scale, EEP data from Ethiopia gives strong evidence that Bitcoin mining has helped [[68|accelerate the building of transmission lines]]. These lines deliver renewable energy to rural communities.
88: In terms of the “use for something better” argument, Bitcoin mining seeks out the cheapest energy. Much of this energy is stranded. Other users cannot use it because of its remote location, unattractive time of day, or both.
94: For example, [[71|Moghimi et al]] found that traditional Microgrids produced a large amount of excess energy. That energy was wasted because renewable generation and demand didn’t match. When Bitcoin mining was added, it prevented almost all energy waste, while cutting microgrid operating costs by 46.5%.

12: On the specific point regarding eWaste, in 2025 Cambridge showed that de Vries’ per transaction method was not only flawed. His total eWaste estimates were also overstated by 1204% (2.3 kT eWaste, not the annual 30 kT eWaste claimed by de Vries). That disproved de Vries’ claim that Bitcoin mining had an eWaste problem.
